newsitem.title: USA: Government says U.S. dengue fever almost doubles.
newsitem.headline: Government says U.S. dengue fever almost doubles.

text.p: Cases of dengue fever increased dramatically in the United States last year as more travelers brought the mosquito-transmitted disease back from the Caribbean, Central America and Mexico, federal health officials said Thursday.

The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said there were 86 laboratory-confirmed cases of the tropical disease in 1995, almost twice the average number reported annually between 1987 and 1994. At least 11 people required hospitalization last year.

There were 22 laboratory-confirmed dengue fever cases just in Texas, which was affected by an epidemic across the border in Mexico. There were 12 cases in New York and eight each in Massachusetts and Oregon.

The disease causes fever, headache, rash, nausea and vomiting and can last up to 10 days. Complete recovery usually occurs within two to four weeks but sometimes it can develop into a more severe form such as dengue haemorrhagic fever.
Illnesses occurred among a group of disaster-relief workers who went from Oregon to St. Thomas in the U.S. Virgin Islands after hurricanes Luis and Marilyn.
The CDC said 49 of last year's cases were probably acquired in the Caribbean, 24 in Mexico and Central America, five in Asia, three in South America and one in Africa.

"All of Central America had increased dengue activity in 1995," said Dr. Jose Rigau of the dengue branch of the CDC's National Centre for Infectious Diseases. "The Caribbean islands also had increased dengue incidence."
Dengue viruses are transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, which are most active during the day. Rigau said outbreaks in the Caribbean generally begin in July or August and end by March.

"There was an ongoing epidemic in Mexico in 1995 with thousands of cases," said Dr. Eduard Sanders, also of the CDC's dengue branch. "In 1994, there was a big epidemic of dengue in Puerto Rico with 25,000 cases."

Health officials said there have been fewer cases of dengue fever this year in tropical regions of the Americas. But travelers to regions where there is a risk of contracting the disease should avoid mosquito bites by using insect repellents on skin and clothing and staying in well-screened or air-conditioned areas, the CDC said.
